_Toxic haze over the Salton Sea. Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair._

Southern California’s Salton Sea was once a [resort
playground](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-vZq7IRxf5w), with sunny [beaches,
celebrities](https://thefern.org/2020/01/as-the-salton-sea-shrinks-it-leaves-
behind-a-toxic-reminder-of-the-cost-of-making-a-desert-bloom/) and people
waterskiing on the vast inland lake in the 1950s and ’60s.

Today, those [resorts are long gone](https://cvindependent.com/2026/01/cv-
history-the-salton-sea-has-gone-from-massive-accident-to-resort-destination-
to-pollution-threat-to-potential-lithium-bonanza/), replaced by a drying and
increasingly toxic landscape. As the lake shrinks, wind blowing across the
exposed lake bed kicks up toxic dust left by years of agriculture chemicals
and metals washing into the lake. That dust makes its way into the lungs of
the children of the Imperial Valley.

New research from [our
team](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=clPzpqIAAAAJ&hl=en) of
[epidemiologists](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=2c4l1pkAAAAJ&hl=en)
at University of Southern California and University of California, Irvine,
shows that [blowing dust is impeding the lung
growth](https://jama.jamanetwork.com/article.aspx?doi=10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.4812)
of children in the region – especially those living closest to the Salton Sea.
In fact, the [effects on lung
function](http://doi.org/10.1097/EE9.0000000000000455) close to the Salton Sea
have been greater than what studies find in [urban California
communities](https://doi.org/10.1136/thoraxjnl-2012-203159) near busy
roadways.

As the lake’s water sources diminish with the region’s Colorado River water
use agreements, and this region gains more industrial activity from proposed
lithium extraction, air pollution is likely to only worsen.

**The problem with the Salton Sea**

The Salton Sea – California’s largest inland lake at [over 340 square
miles](https://saltonsea.com/about/faq/) – has been shrinking for decades due
to drought, agricultural water diversion and climate change. Its was created
by a [break in a
canal](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12583-016-0630-7) carrying
water from the Colorado River in the early 1900s. Irrigation runoff from farm
fields kept it going. But over the past two decades, [decreasing water flow
has exposed 36,000 new acres of dry lake bed](https://pacinst.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/08/SaltonSeaAQ_Final.pdf), which release large amounts of
dust into the air.

The lake sits [235 feet below sea level](https://saltonsea.com/get-
informed/facts/) in one of the hottest and driest parts of California,
approximately 150 miles southeast of Los Angeles and at the northern border of
the highly productive agricultural region known as the Imperial Valley.

Its water level has been [maintained primarily by agriculture irrigation
runoff](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12583-016-0630-7), which
carries with it [fertilizers, pesticides, salt and toxic
metals](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2016.03.144). Those chemicals,
salts and metals have concentrated over time in the lake bed sediments, and
they get stirred up into the air when the wind blows through.

As the [largest
consumer](https://www.iid.com/Home/Components/News/News/1369/30) of Colorado
River water, Imperial County’s irrigation district agreed in 2003 to [forgo
billions of gallons of
water](https://web.archive.org/web/20141111143751/http:/iid.com/index.aspx?page=122)
every year to support growing urban areas – a plan that went into full effect
in 2018. That meant less runoff into the lake. By one estimate, the change was
projected to [increase windblown dust by 40 to 80 tons per
day](https://pacinst.org/publication/restoration-project-critical-to-salton-
seas-future/). Satellite images show rapid expansion of exposed lake bed as
the water has receded.

The shrinking of the Salton Sea, 1984 to 2022.

The [predominantly low-income Latino
communities](https://theconversation.com/big-lithium-plans-for-imperial-
valley-one-of-californias-poorest-regions-raise-a-bigger-question-who-should-
benefit-238397) that live just south of the Salton Sea say they [have long
been overlooked](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20116023) in conversations
about the lake’s fate. Yet, these communities are facing real health
consequences tied directly to regional water policy choices and lack of action
to manage this emerging environmental crisis.

## Lung damage and slower lung growth

In 2017, we initiated the [Assessing Imperial Valley Respiratory Health and
the Environment, or
AIRE](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/ppe.13065), cohort
study with over 700 elementary school-age children across five northern
Imperial Valley cities.

The study was built on a partnership with [Comité Cívico del
Valle](https://ccvhealth.org/), a local nonprofit that has been active in
addressing community health and environmental concerns in the Imperial Valley
region.

Our study followed these children over several years, documenting respiratory
health symptoms and lung function measurements, in addition to household,
lifestyle and behavioral factors to account for individual differences.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/04/lungprobsalton-680x468.png)

Our [initial findings](https://www.mdpi.com/1660-4601/16/20/3828) aligned with
what [local residents have discussed for
years](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20116023):

> \+ Among children living in the northern Imperial Valley, nearly 1 in 5 are
> reported as having asthma – far higher than the [national
> rate](https://www.lung.org/research/trends-in-lung-disease/asthma-trends-
> brief/current-demographics).
>
> \+ Higher rates of air pollution were linked to overall poorer reported
> [respiratory
> health](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0013935124019777),
> such as wheezing and coughing, among all children. That indicates that while
> asthmatic children were more sensitive, nonasthmatic children experienced
> significant health impacts as well.
>
> \+ Our work has also begun to show that higher levels of dust exposure,
> especially among those children living closer to the sea, are linked to
> [poorer lung function](https://academic.oup.com/ajrccm/article-
> abstract/211/11/2133/8444167?__cf_chl_rt_tk=kQaWbdcB1HX2OffFsNUKdSBg3Mmntygh8Hoc7jvBG78-1773852573-1.0.1.1-J_gCYx7KScS95bgnoAGjIXNHMOKiPdknMFstNQbkMPM),
> as well as reductions in children’s lung growth over time. Reduced lung
> function increases the risk for chronic respiratory disease, such as COPD,
> or more frequent respiratory infections, such as pneumonia, as adults.

These findings are concerning because lung damage, poor lung function and
respiratory illness in early life may [increase the risk of chronic health
problems](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jped.2021.11.005) into adulthood.

Children’s [lungs are still
developing](https://www.connecticutchildrens.org/growing-healthy/breathing-
emergency-how-recognize-and-respond-respiratory-distress), and lung function
continues to mature throughout adolescence, making children more susceptible
than adults to the adverse impacts of air pollution.

Children also have [higher respiratory rates](https://www.lung.org/clean-
air/outdoors/who-is-at-risk) than adults, as well as larger lung surface area
relative to their body size, resulting in higher doses of pollution per
breath. And since children often spend more time outdoors than many adults and
tend to engage in more physical activity, that may increase their exposure to
outdoor air pollution.

**Looking ahead**

For years, community members have [raised concerns about the high rates of
asthma](https://www.ccvhealth.org/asthma-intervention) and poor respiratory
health among children and residents.

While questions remain about the longer-term impacts of worsening air quality
related to the drying Salton Sea, our study adds scientific backing to
residents’ experiences. This evidence matters as communities and organizations
like Comité Cívico del Valle push for projects that can [reduce the amount of
Salton Sea dust](https://saltonsea.ca.gov/program/) that gets into the air,
expand education on asthma management and increase access to health care
services.

The kids in the AIRE study were just starting elementary school when they
joined. Now in high school, this generation has grown up near the Salton Sea.
Many have [dealt with asthma and may face chronic health
problems](https://jama.jamanetwork.com/article.aspx?doi=10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.4812).

From everything we have seen in the results of our studies involving the
children living in communities along the Salton Sea, we believe the protection
of local air quality is critical for the health of children in the Imperial
Valley, and their health should be in the forefront of planning for future
water changes, extraction projects and other development near the Salton
Sea.![The
